title: Congenital and Genetic Reproductive Diseases
subject: Reproductive System (REPR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers reproductive disorders that are present from conception or birth: chromosomal and single-gene disorders (Turner, Klinefelter, fragile X, androgen insensitivity), disorders of sex development, and structural malformations of the testis, penis, foreskin, uterus, vagina, and hymen. Each one makes sense once you know two things: which embryologic step failed, and what happened to the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal feedback loop as a result. Board questions usually give a karyotype, a physical finding, or a hormone panel and ask you to name the condition or predict the missing piece, so the chapter keeps returning to those two questions.
prerequisites: Gonadal, ductal, and external genital development, including SRY, AMH, testosterone, and DHT
Hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis: GnRH, LH, FSH, inhibin B, and sex steroid feedback
Testicular histology: Sertoli cells, Leydig cells, and spermatogenesis
Meiotic nondisjunction, X inactivation, and X-linked inheritance
Adrenal steroid synthesis pathway and the role of ACTH

connections.how: Every malformation in this chapter is a specific failure of fusion, resorption, canalization, or descent described in normal development.
21-hydroxylase deficiency is the commonest cause of 46,XX DSD and links genital ambiguity to cortisol, aldosterone, and ACTH physiology.
Fragile X shows how an unstable repeat, promoter methylation, and parent-of-origin expansion produce anticipation.
Turner syndrome is a classic cause of bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of the aorta.

connections.to: Reproductive neoplasia: testicular germ cell tumors
connections.how: Cryptorchidism and gonads with Y material carry a raised risk of germ cell tumors.

terms.def: A congenital condition in which chromosomal, gonadal, or anatomic sex is atypical or does not match.
Low gonadal hormone output from primary gonadal failure, with high LH and FSH because negative feedback is lost.
A glycoprotein from Sertoli cells (and granulosa cells in the ovary) that selectively suppresses pituitary FSH secretion.
A Sertoli cell hormone that causes regression of the paramesonephric (Mullerian) ducts in the male fetus.
The potent androgen formed from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase that masculinizes the external genitalia and prostate.
A gonad reduced to fibrous ovarian-type stroma without follicles or germ cells.
Earlier onset or greater severity of a genetic disorder in successive generations, typically from expansion of a repeat.
An FMR1 allele of about 55 to 200 CGG repeats that is still expressed but is unstable when transmitted by a female.
Accumulation of menstrual blood within the vagina behind an obstruction.
A proposed grouping of cryptorchidism, hypospadias, poor semen quality, and testicular germ cell tumors attributed to abnormal fetal testis development.
A growth gene in the pseudoautosomal region of the X and Y chromosomes that escapes X inactivation, so two active copies are normal.

blocks.text: Cryptorchidism is failure of one or both testes to reach the scrotum. Descent occurs in two phases. In the transabdominal phase, insulin-like peptide 3 (INSL3) from Leydig cells enlarges the gubernaculum, which anchors the testis near the deep inguinal ring as the abdomen grows. In the inguinoscrotal phase, androgen-dependent migration of the gubernaculum carries the testis through the inguinal canal, usually reaching the scrotum by the last weeks of gestation.

Because the final phase is late, preterm infants are affected far more often than term infants, and many undescended testes still descend during the first few months of life, aided by the postnatal surge of gonadotropins and testosterone. Most undescended testes lie in the inguinal canal; fewer are intra-abdominal or high scrotal. The condition is usually unilateral. A retractile testis, which can be brought into the scrotum but is pulled up by an active cremasteric reflex, is a normal variant and must be distinguished. A patent processus vaginalis often accompanies the defect, so an indirect inguinal hernia is a common association.
Why spermatogenesis and hormone levels change

Spermatogenesis needs a temperature about 2 to 3 °C (3.6 to 5.4 °F) below core body temperature, which the scrotum and the pampiniform plexus countercurrent exchanger provide. A testis held in the canal or abdomen is warmer, so germ cells are lost progressively after the first year and the tubules become small and fibrotic. Sertoli cells are also heat sensitive and make less inhibin B, so FSH rises. Leydig cells tolerate heat better, so testosterone is usually normal, particularly when one testis is normal. Infertility is therefore most likely when both testes are undescended.

Germ cells in an undescended testis mature abnormally, and germ cell neoplasia in situ can develop, giving a several-fold higher risk of testicular germ cell tumor, most often seminoma. The contralateral, normally descended testis also carries a modestly raised risk, which suggests that a shared intrinsic defect of fetal testis development, and not temperature alone, contributes. This idea underlies the testicular dysgenesis syndrome concept (C02).

blocks.predict: A man with bilateral intra-abdominal testes has a semen analysis showing azoospermia. Predict his FSH, inhibin B, LH, and testosterone.
blocks.explain: Inhibin B is low and FSH high because heat damages Sertoli cells and germ cells. Leydig cells tolerate heat better, so testosterone is usually normal or only mildly low, with LH normal or mildly raised.
blocks.check: The paragraph on temperature, Sertoli cells, and Leydig cells.

blocks.text: The male external genitalia develop from indifferent structures under the influence of DHT. The genital tubercle elongates to form the phallus, and the urethral folds on its ventral surface fuse in the midline from proximal to distal, enclosing the urethral groove to form the penile urethra. The labioscrotal swellings fuse behind them to form the scrotum. Any failure of androgen production or action during this window can stop fusion part way.

Hypospadias is an opening of the urethra on the ventral (under) surface of the penis because the urethral folds failed to fuse completely. It is one of the commonest congenital anomalies in boys, at about 1 in 250 live male births. Most openings are distal, near the glans or corona; proximal openings on the shaft, scrotum, or perineum reflect earlier, more severe failure. A ventral curvature of the penis (chordee) and a hooded, incomplete foreskin often accompany it. Because the same androgen-dependent window governs testicular descent and closure of the processus vaginalis, hypospadias is associated with cryptorchidism and inguinal hernia. Severe hypospadias together with an undescended testis raises the possibility of a disorder of sex development (C07), including a virilized 46,XX infant with congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

Epispadias is an opening on the dorsal (upper) surface. It is not a fusion failure of the urethral folds but a different and much rarer error: the genital tubercle forms in an abnormal position, related to defective development of the infraumbilical abdominal wall and cloacal membrane. For this reason epispadias is usually part of the bladder exstrophy and epispadias complex, in which the bladder is open on the lower abdominal wall and the pubic bones are widely separated. When the defect reaches the bladder neck, the sphincter mechanism is incomplete and urinary incontinence results.

blocks.text: Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability. It is caused by expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat in the 5' untranslated region of the FMR1 gene at Xq27.3. Inheritance is X-linked (often described as X-linked dominant with reduced penetrance), so males are more severely affected and females with a full mutation show variable, usually milder, features because of random X inactivation.

Normal alleles have fewer than about 45 repeats. When an allele exceeds about 200 repeats (the full mutation), the repeat and the FMR1 promoter become hypermethylated, chromatin condenses, and transcription stops. The missing protein, FMRP, is an RNA-binding protein that normally restrains local translation of synaptic messenger RNAs in dendrites. Without it, excess synaptic protein synthesis leaves dendritic spines long, thin, and immature, which underlies the intellectual disability, autism features, and attention problems.

blocks.title: From repeat expansion to disease
steps: Full mutation over about 200 repeats in the child
Hypermethylation of repeat and FMR1 promoter
Unrestrained synaptic translation, immature dendritic spines
Intellectual disability and the fragile X phenotype
blocks.caption: The repeat expands through the mother; methylation, not a change in protein sequence, causes loss of function.

blocks.text: Anticipation follows from the instability of the repeat in female meiosis. A mother with a premutation can pass a full mutation to her child, and the larger her repeat, the higher that risk. A male with a premutation passes it to all his daughters, usually without expansion, and to none of his sons. Premutation alleles are still transcribed, and excess FMR1 messenger RNA is thought to be toxic: female carriers are at risk of primary ovarian insufficiency, and older male carriers of fragile X associated tremor and ataxia syndrome.

Affected males have intellectual disability, a long narrow face, a large prominent jaw, large protruding ears, and joint hypermobility, and some have mitral valve prolapse. Macroorchidism, meaning testes clearly larger than normal for age, usually appears after puberty, so it is a clue in an adolescent or adult and not in a young child.

The upper vagina comes from the fused paramesonephric ducts, and the lower vagina from the sinovaginal bulbs of the urogenital sinus, which form a solid vaginal plate. The plate canalizes, and a thin membrane, the hymen, remains between the vaginal lumen and the urogenital sinus (future vestibule). It normally perforates during late fetal life. Imperforate hymen is persistence of that membrane without an opening, and it is the most common obstructive anomaly of the female genital tract.

The ovaries, uterus, and hypothalamic-pituitary axis are all normal, so the girl goes through a normal puberty with breast development and pubic hair. The problem appears only when menstruation begins. Endometrium sheds on schedule, but the blood has no exit, so it collects behind the membrane. She presents with primary amenorrhea despite normal secondary sexual characteristics, together with cyclic lower abdominal or pelvic pain that recurs each month. Examination shows a tense, bulging membrane at the introitus that looks bluish because dark blood lies behind it, and it bulges further with straining.

blocks.title: Imperforate hymen at menarche
steps: Pelvic mass compresses bladder and rectum
blocks.caption: Each cycle adds blood above the obstruction, so pain and mass effect worsen over months.

blocks.text: As blood accumulates, the distended vagina (hematocolpos) can form a lower abdominal mass, and pressure on the urethra and rectum can cause urinary retention and constipation. Further accumulation distends the uterus and tubes, and retrograde flow through the tubes raises the risk of endometriosis. In a newborn, maternal estrogen can stimulate enough vaginal secretion to produce a bulging mucocolpos, so the anomaly is sometimes found at birth. A transverse vaginal septum (C10) gives the same history, but the obstruction lies higher in the vagina, so no bulging membrane is seen at the introitus.

Klinefelter syndrome is the most common chromosomal cause of male hypogonadism and infertility, affecting about 1 in 600 males. The 47,XXY karyotype arises from meiotic nondisjunction in either parent, and mosaic 46,XY/47,XXY forms are milder. The Y chromosome carries SRY, so testes form and the infant looks male, while the extra X is inactivated and seen as a Barr body. Testicular failure is thought to reflect an extra dose of genes that escape X inactivation, which disrupts the germ cells and Sertoli cells of the seminiferous tubules.

Two separate compartments of the testis fail, and each produces its own hormone signature. Tubular failure (seminiferous tubule dysgenesis) means germ cells are lost and tubules become hyalinized, so Sertoli cells make little inhibin B and FSH rises sharply; the result is azoospermia. Leydig cell dysfunction means testosterone is low or low-normal, so the hypothalamus and pituitary lose negative feedback and LH rises. The Leydig cells often look clumped or hyperplastic on biopsy because the tubules around them have shrunk, but they function poorly.

blocks.title: Feedback loss in Klinefelter syndrome
steps: High LH drives aromatase, estradiol rises relative to testosterone
Gonads cannot respond, so gonadotropins stay high
blocks.caption: Primary testicular failure: the pituitary signals harder, but the testis cannot answer.

blocks.text: The physical findings follow from this hormone pattern. The testes are small and firm because tubules are scarred, and this is the most consistent sign. Low testosterone delays closure of the epiphyses, and the extra copy of the pseudoautosomal SHOX gene adds growth, so patients are tall with long legs and an arm span exceeding height (eunuchoid proportions). High LH stimulates aromatization, so estradiol is high relative to testosterone and gynecomastia develops. Facial and body hair may be sparse with a female-type pubic hair pattern.

Intelligence is usually in the normal range, but language and learning difficulties are more common. The altered estrogen to androgen ratio raises the risk of male breast cancer, low testosterone contributes to osteoporosis, and the risks of extragonadal (mediastinal) germ cell tumors and of some autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus are increased.

blocks.predict: Why is FSH raised more consistently than LH in Klinefelter syndrome, even in men whose testosterone is in the low-normal range?
blocks.explain: FSH is restrained mainly by inhibin B, which falls as soon as the tubules fail. LH is restrained by testosterone, so if Leydig cells still make enough testosterone, LH may be only mildly raised.
blocks.check: The two compartments paragraph and the feedback cycle.

blocks.text: The prepuce (foreskin) is a fold of skin and mucosa that covers the glans. At birth its inner surface is normally adherent to the glans, and its opening is narrow. The adhesions separate gradually, so retractability increases through childhood and is present in most boys by adolescence.

Phimosis is a foreskin that cannot be retracted over the glans. In infants and young boys it is physiologic, and the foreskin is soft and unscarred. Acquired (pathologic) phimosis results from scarring that forms a tight, often white, fibrous ring at the tip of the foreskin. Causes include recurrent balanoposthitis (inflammation of the glans and foreskin), which is more common with poor hygiene and with diabetes because glucose in urine favors Candida, as well as lichen sclerosus and tears from forceful retraction. The narrow opening traps smegma and urine, causing ballooning of the foreskin on voiding, further infection, and occasionally urinary obstruction. Chronic inflammation under a nonretractile foreskin is a recognized risk factor for penile squamous cell carcinoma.

Paraphimosis is the opposite situation: a foreskin that has been retracted behind the corona cannot be returned over the glans. It often follows retraction for cleaning, examination, or urinary catheter placement when the foreskin is not replaced. A relatively tight foreskin then acts as a constricting band. Low-pressure veins and lymphatics are compressed first, so the glans and the distal foreskin swell, the swelling tightens the band further, and eventually arterial inflow is threatened. The result is a painful, swollen glans with a tight ring behind it, which can progress to ischemia and necrosis. That self-reinforcing loop is why paraphimosis is an emergency while phimosis usually is not.

blocks.text: Sexual differentiation proceeds in a fixed order, and each level depends on a different signal. Chromosomes decide the gonad: SRY on the Y chromosome directs the bipotential gonad to become a testis, and without it an ovary forms. The gonad then decides the ducts through its hormones. The external genitalia depend on androgen, specifically DHT, and form female in its absence. A disorder of sex development (DSD) occurs when one of these steps fails, so the gonads and the external genitalia do not match.

blocks.title: Normal male sexual differentiation
steps: Sertoli cells secrete AMH: Mullerian ducts regress
Leydig cells secrete testosterone: Wolffian ducts persist
DHT masculinizes external genitalia and prostate
blocks.caption: Without SRY, no AMH, and no androgen, the default is ovaries, Mullerian structures, and female external genitalia.

blocks.text: In 46,XX DSD the karyotype is female, the gonads are ovaries, and the uterus and tubes are normal because no AMH was ever made. The external genitalia are virilized because the fetus was exposed to androgen. The most common cause is congenital adrenal hyperplasia from 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Low cortisol removes negative feedback on the pituitary, so ACTH rises and drives the adrenal cortex; precursors that cannot become cortisol or aldosterone are shunted into adrenal androgens. The newborn has clitoromegaly and fused labioscrotal folds, and in the salt-wasting form, aldosterone deficiency causes hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypovolemia in the first weeks. Excess maternal androgen from an ovarian or adrenal tumor, or exogenous androgen, has the same effect on the fetus. Androgen exposure before about 12 weeks fuses the labioscrotal folds, while later exposure enlarges only the clitoris.

In 46,XY DSD the karyotype is male and testes are present, so AMH works and Mullerian structures are absent, but the external genitalia are undervirilized because testosterone was not converted or did not act. Androgen insensitivity (C08) is a receptor defect. In 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency, an autosomal recessive disorder, testosterone is normal and builds the Wolffian structures (epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles), but too little DHT is made to masculinize the external genitalia, so the infant has ambiguous or female-appearing genitalia. At puberty the large rise in testosterone causes substantial virilization.

blocks.title: 46,XX DSD compared with 46,XY DSD
rows: 21-hydroxylase deficiency; maternal androgen-secreting tumor or exogenous androgen
blocks.caption: The gonad names the category; the external genitalia show which way androgen exposure went wrong.

blocks.title: Reading the testosterone to DHT ratio
blocks.text: A 46,XY infant has ambiguous genitalia, palpable inguinal testes, and no uterus on ultrasound. Testes and absent uterus confirm functioning Sertoli cells and AMH. Testosterone is normal for age, so Leydig cells work. The question is whether androgen is not converted or not sensed. The testosterone to DHT ratio is high, which points to 5-alpha-reductase deficiency: testosterone is present, but little DHT is formed. In androgen insensitivity the ratio is normal and LH is high because the hypothalamus cannot sense testosterone. Wolffian structures help as well: present in 5-alpha-reductase deficiency (testosterone acts directly) but absent or rudimentary in complete androgen insensitivity (no working receptor).

Complete androgen insensitivity is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the androgen receptor gene on the X chromosome, inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern. The person is 46,XY with normal testes, which make normal or high amounts of testosterone and normal AMH. Every tissue fails to respond to testosterone and DHT, so the phenotype is defined by which steps of differentiation need androgen and which do not.

AMH acts through its own receptor, so the Mullerian ducts regress and the uterus, tubes, and upper vagina are absent. The Wolffian ducts need testosterone acting on the androgen receptor, so they also regress. The external genitalia, lacking DHT action, develop as female, and the lower vagina forms from the urogenital sinus as a short blind pouch. The testes do not descend into a scrotum and lie in the abdomen, inguinal canal, or labia majora; an inguinal hernia containing a testis in an apparently female infant is a classic early presentation.

Most cases present at puberty with primary amenorrhea in a girl who has developed breasts. Breast development is explained by aromatization: testosterone is converted to estradiol in peripheral tissues, and there is no androgen effect to oppose estrogen at the breast. Pubic and axillary hair depend on androgen, so they are sparse or absent.

The hormone pattern reflects resistance at the hypothalamus and pituitary. Testosterone normally suppresses LH through the androgen receptor, so with no working receptor the feedback signal is not sensed, LH rises, and the Leydig cells are driven to make testosterone in the male range or higher. More testosterone means more aromatization, so estradiol is high for a male. FSH is often normal or only mildly raised because inhibin B from Sertoli cells still restrains it. The undescended testes carry an increased risk of germ cell tumor that rises after puberty. Partial androgen insensitivity, from a receptor with some residual function, produces a spectrum from ambiguous genitalia to an undervirilized male.

blocks.title: Which structures need which hormone, and what happens in complete androgen insensitivity
rows: No uterus, tubes, or upper vagina
Female external genitalia, blind vaginal pouch
blocks.caption: Everything that needs the androgen receptor fails; everything driven by AMH or estrogen proceeds.

sections.title: Mullerian agenesis compared with complete androgen insensitivity

blocks.text: Mullerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome) is congenital absence of the uterus and upper vagina in a 46,XX female. The paramesonephric ducts fail to develop or fuse, so the uterus is absent or present only as small rudimentary buds, and the upper two-thirds of the vagina is missing. The lower vagina comes from the urogenital sinus, so a short blind vaginal pouch is present. The cause is not established and most cases are sporadic. It is one of the leading causes of primary amenorrhea, after gonadal dysgenesis such as Turner syndrome.

The ovaries develop from the genital ridge, not from the Mullerian ducts, so they are normal. They ovulate and make estradiol, so breast development, the pubertal growth spurt, and pubic and axillary hair (from normal adrenal and ovarian androgens acting on normal receptors) are all typical of a female. FSH, LH, estradiol, and testosterone are in the normal female range. The only complaint is absent menses, sometimes with cyclic symptoms from normal ovarian cycling. Because the Mullerian and Wolffian ducts develop next to the forming kidney, renal anomalies such as unilateral renal agenesis or a pelvic kidney are common, and vertebral anomalies also occur.

Complete androgen insensitivity (C08) produces the same picture at first glance: a phenotypic girl with breasts, primary amenorrhea, no uterus, and a blind vaginal pouch. Two findings separate them at the bedside, and two separate them in the laboratory. Pubic and axillary hair is normal in Mullerian agenesis but sparse in androgen insensitivity, and gonads may be palpable in the groin only in androgen insensitivity. Testosterone is in the female range in Mullerian agenesis but in the male range in androgen insensitivity, and the karyotype settles the question.

blocks.title: Primary amenorrhea with a blind vaginal pouch
rows: Inguinal hernia, gonadal germ cell tumor risk
blocks.caption: Same pelvis, different reason: one never formed the ducts, the other formed testes that removed them.

blocks.title: Working through primary amenorrhea
blocks.text: A 16-year-old has never menstruated. First ask whether there is breast development, which shows estrogen exposure. No breasts with high FSH means gonadal failure, as in Turner syndrome (C11). Breasts present means estrogen is being made, so look for an outflow problem. If a uterus is present and a bluish bulge is seen at the introitus with monthly pain, think of imperforate hymen (C04). If the uterus is absent and the vagina ends in a blind pouch, check pubic hair and testosterone: normal hair and female-range testosterone mean Mullerian agenesis; sparse hair and male-range testosterone mean complete androgen insensitivity.

The uterus and upper vagina form in three steps. The paired paramesonephric ducts grow down and fuse in the midline, so for a time the fused segment has a wall down its center. That midline septum is then resorbed, leaving a single cavity, and the vaginal plate canalizes to open the lower vagina. Each step can fail in its own way, and the step that failed predicts the anatomy.

A septate uterus results when the ducts fuse normally but the midline septum is not resorbed. The external contour of the fundus is smooth and normal, because fusion was complete, while the cavity is divided by a partial or complete septum. This distinguishes it from a bicornuate uterus, in which fusion itself was incomplete and the fundus is indented. Septate uterus is the most common structural uterine anomaly and the one most strongly linked to recurrent pregnancy loss. The septum is fibromuscular tissue with a poorer blood supply than normal myometrium, so an embryo that implants on it has inadequate placentation and is more likely to be lost, usually in the first or early second trimester. Preterm birth and malpresentation are also more common.

A longitudinal vaginal septum is a midline wall running down the vagina, produced by incomplete fusion of the lower paramesonephric ducts or failure of the septum between them to resorb. It often coexists with a septate uterus or a uterus didelphys and may cause dyspareunia or difficulty with tampon use. If one side is blocked, menstrual blood collects in an obstructed hemivagina, which is classically associated with absence of the kidney on the same side. A transverse vaginal septum is a horizontal membrane caused by failed fusion or canalization where the Mullerian-derived upper vagina meets the sinus-derived vaginal plate. It obstructs menstrual flow like an imperforate hymen, with primary amenorrhea, cyclic pain, and hematocolpos, but the hymen is normal and no bulge appears at the introitus.

blocks.text: Turner syndrome is the absence of all or part of one X chromosome in a phenotypic female, affecting about 1 in 2,500 live-born girls. About half have a 45,X karyotype, usually from loss of the paternal X; the rest are mosaic (for example 45,X/46,XX) or carry a structurally abnormal X such as an isochromosome of the long arm. Most 45,X conceptions are lost in pregnancy. With only one X there is no Barr body. Turner syndrome is the most common cause of primary amenorrhea and the classic example of gonadal dysgenesis.

Germ cells reach the fetal ovary and oocytes form, but maintaining them requires genes on both X chromosomes. With a single X, oocytes undergo accelerated atresia, mostly before birth, and the ovaries are reduced to streak gonads of fibrous stroma with no follicles. Without follicles, the granulosa and theca cells that make estradiol and inhibin are absent.

The hormone pattern is hypergonadotropic hypogonadism. Estradiol is low, so there is no breast development and no menarche, giving primary amenorrhea with absent thelarche. Loss of estradiol and inhibin removes negative feedback, so FSH and LH are both high, with FSH typically higher. The uterus is present because no AMH was made, but it stays small without estrogen. Pubic and axillary hair can appear because adrenal androgens at adrenarche are normal. Low estrogen also leads to poor bone mineralization.

Mosaic patients may retain enough follicles to start puberty and even menstruate before the ovaries fail early, so Turner syndrome can also present as secondary amenorrhea with premature ovarian insufficiency. When any Y chromosome material is present in a mosaic karyotype, the dysgenetic gonad has a substantial risk of gonadoblastoma.

blocks.title: Gonadotropin patterns in this chapter
blocks.caption: Low inhibin B tracks tubular or follicular loss and raises FSH; loss of steroid feedback or receptor resistance raises LH.

blocks.predict: A 15-year-old with no breast development has high FSH and LH. Another has no breast development with low FSH and LH. Which has Turner syndrome, and where is the lesion in the other?
blocks.explain: The first. High gonadotropins mean the pituitary is signaling but the gonad cannot respond (primary failure). Low gonadotropins point to the hypothalamus or pituitary, as in constitutional delay or Kallmann syndrome.
blocks.check: The hormone pattern paragraph and the gonadotropin table.

blocks.text: Most of the nonovarian findings of Turner syndrome trace to two causes: too little of a dosage-sensitive growth gene, and abnormal development of the fetal lymphatic system. Short stature is the most consistent feature. It results from haploinsufficiency of SHOX, a gene in the pseudoautosomal region of the X chromosome that escapes X inactivation, so a normal female has two working copies and a woman with 45,X has one. Growth is slow throughout childhood with no pubertal spurt, and skeletal signs from the same cause include a wide carrying angle at the elbow (cubitus valgus) and short fourth metacarpals. Klinefelter syndrome shows the converse, with three copies and tall stature (C05).

In the fetus, the jugular lymph sacs fail to connect normally to the venous system, so lymph accumulates in the neck as a cystic hygroma, which can be seen on prenatal ultrasound. When it later regresses, it leaves redundant skin folds that form the webbed neck and a low posterior hairline. Generalized lymphatic hypoplasia produces lymphedema of the hands and feet that is often present at birth and is a key neonatal clue. A broad shield chest with widely spaced nipples is also typical.

Cardiovascular anomalies are the most important cause of serious complications. A bicuspid aortic valve is the most common, and coarctation of the aorta is the classic association, which explains hypertension and weak femoral pulses in a girl. One proposed explanation is that distended fetal lymphatics compress the developing outflow tract and reduce flow through the left heart, but this remains a hypothesis. Aortic dilation and dissection are later risks, made more likely by these lesions and by hypertension. The commonest renal anomaly is a horseshoe kidney, in which the lower poles fuse and ascent is halted beneath the inferior mesenteric artery. Autoimmune hypothyroidism and hearing loss are also more common.

integration.text: Embryology explains the anatomy in this chapter. The same few signals, SRY, AMH, testosterone, and DHT, decide the gonad, the ducts, and the external genitalia, so a karyotype plus three questions (which gonad, is there a uterus, how virilized are the genitalia) localizes most disorders of sex development. Structural defects follow the specific step that failed: descent in cryptorchidism, fold fusion in hypospadias, tubercle position in epispadias, duct formation in Mullerian agenesis, resorption in septate uterus, and canalization or perforation in vaginal septa and imperforate hymen. Because the paramesonephric ducts develop beside the forming kidney, Mullerian anomalies often travel with renal anomalies.

Physiology and genetics explain the laboratory findings. Inhibin B reports on Sertoli and granulosa cells and governs FSH, while sex steroids and their receptors govern LH, so a hormone panel shows which compartment failed. Genetic mechanisms differ in instructive ways: whole chromosome gain or loss with gene dosage effects in Klinefelter and Turner syndromes, an unstable repeat with methylation silencing in fragile X, and a receptor defect in androgen insensitivity. Hormone values vary with age, pubertal stage, and laboratory, so patterns are more reliable than single cutoffs, and the karyotype is the final arbiter when phenotypes overlap.

summary: Cryptorchidism is most often inguinal and more common in preterm infants; heat damages germ cells and Sertoli cells, lowering inhibin B and raising FSH, and germ cell tumor risk is increased.
Hypospadias is a ventral meatus from incomplete urethral fold fusion with cryptorchidism and hernia; epispadias is a dorsal meatus from a malpositioned genital tubercle with bladder exstrophy.

Fragile X is an FMR1 CGG expansion beyond about 200 repeats that is methylated and silenced; it expands through the mother and causes intellectual disability, long face, large jaw and ears, and postpubertal macroorchidism.
Imperforate hymen gives primary amenorrhea with normal puberty, cyclic pain, a bulging bluish membrane, and hematocolpos.

Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) combines tubular failure (low inhibin B, high FSH, azoospermia) with Leydig failure (low testosterone, high LH), giving small firm testes, tall stature, and gynecomastia.
Phimosis is a foreskin that cannot retract, physiologic in infancy or from scarring; paraphimosis is a retracted foreskin trapped behind the glans that obstructs venous return and threatens ischemia.

46,XX DSD means ovaries with virilized genitalia from excess androgen (most often 21-hydroxylase deficiency); 46,XY DSD means testes with undervirilized genitalia from failed androgen action or DHT synthesis.
Complete androgen insensitivity gives female external genitalia, a blind pouch, no uterus, undescended testes, sparse hair, and high testosterone, estradiol, and LH.
Mullerian agenesis (46,XX) has normal ovaries, hair, and female hormone levels with absent uterus and upper vagina, often with renal anomalies.

Turner syndrome (45,X or mosaic) causes streak ovaries with low estradiol and high FSH and LH, plus short stature (SHOX), webbed neck, lymphedema, bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, and horseshoe kidney.

verify: Incidence figures (cryptorchidism by gestational age, hypospadias about 1 in 250 male births, Klinefelter about 1 in 600 males, Turner about 1 in 2,500 female births, imperforate hymen about 1 in 1,000 to 2,000) vary between sources; confirm the values NABNE expects.

Hormone pattern in cryptorchidism: some review sources state that testosterone falls and LH rises in bilateral cryptorchidism, while others state testosterone is usually normal; this chapter states usually normal with normal or mildly raised LH.
The magnitude of germ cell tumor risk in cryptorchidism is quoted from about 3 to 10 times baseline; the chapter says several-fold.
FMR1 repeat thresholds (normal under about 45, intermediate about 45 to 54, premutation about 55 to 200, full mutation over about 200) differ slightly between laboratories and texts.
Fragile X inheritance is described as X-linked dominant in some review sources and simply X-linked in genetics texts; confirm the label NABNE uses.
The mechanism of macroorchidism in fragile X is not fully established, so the chapter does not state one.
Frequencies of bicuspid aortic valve (about 15% to 30%) and coarctation (about 5% to 15%) in Turner syndrome differ by series and were left out of the text.
The lymphatic compression hypothesis for left-sided heart lesions in Turner syndrome is presented as a proposed mechanism only.

Confirm whether NABNE uses the eponym Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome and the term OHVIRA for obstructed hemivagina with ipsilateral renal agenesis (the chapter describes the latter without the acronym).

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: sex-differentiation (bipotential gonad, ducts, and external genitalia with SRY, AMH, testosterone, and DHT labeled) and uterine-anomalies (septate, bicornuate, didelphys, unicornuate outlines).
